name: ngrok
summary: A small agent dials out from your laptop, server or cluster to ngrok’s network, which gives the service a public URL and carries its traffic back down that connection.
intro: You run an agent next to the service: the `ngrok` command, an Agent SDK inside your app, the Kubernetes Operator, or plain `ssh -R`. It opens one long-lived, outbound TLS connection to ngrok on port 443, called a session, and asks ngrok to create endpoints on it. `ngrok http 8080` returns a public HTTPS URL with a certificate ngrok provisions. Requests land at one of ngrok’s eight points of presence (Ohio, California, São Paulo, Frankfurt, Mumbai, Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney) and travel back down the session to `localhost:8080`. `ngrok tcp` and `ngrok tls` carry databases, SSH and RDP the same way. Nothing listens on your machine, so it works behind NAT and firewalls that block inbound traffic.

An agent endpoint lives only as long as its session: stop the agent and the URL stops answering. Cloud Endpoints are configured centrally and stay up with no process of yours running, and two endpoints with the same URL form a pool that shares traffic. Authentication, IP rules, rewrites and rate limits are written as a Traffic Policy, which ngrok applies in its own network before traffic reaches the agent, so the same rules work whichever kind of agent created the endpoint. ngrok now sells this as Gateway, next to an AI Gateway for model providers, with Share Localhost, the original use, as the third product.
strengths: No inbound port, public IP or firewall change: one outbound TLS connection on port 443 works from home Wi-Fi and locked-down corporate networks, and the session lets you restart or upgrade an agent from the dashboard or API
Built for webhooks and demos: `ngrok http 8080` gives an HTTPS URL at once, and the inspector at `localhost:4040` shows every request’s headers and body and can replay it
One model from laptop to production: the CLI, Agent SDKs for Python, JavaScript, Go, Rust and Java, and a Kubernetes Operator that turns Ingress and Gateway API resources into endpoints
Traffic Policy moves auth, IP restrictions and rate limiting out of the app, and nobody can go around ngrok to the origin because it has no public address
limits: The free plan allows 1 GB of transfer, 20,000 HTTP requests and 5,000 TCP connections a month, up to 3 online endpoints on one assigned dev domain, and shows an interstitial warning page to browser visitors
Agent endpoints go offline when the agent does; staying up takes a service install, a reserved domain, a pool of agents or a Cloud Endpoint

Paid use is metered: Pay-as-you-go is $20 a month with $20 of usage included, then $0.10 per GB out, $1 per 100,000 HTTP requests, endpoint hours and Traffic Policy units; on the $10 Hobbyist plan endpoints stop when the credit runs out
Every request hairpins through a third party’s eight regions, and ngrok terminates TLS for HTTPS endpoints unless you set up TLS termination at the agent; the local inspector only covers HTTP

story: Webhooks need a public address: a service such as Twilio calls your HTTP server when something happens, and a laptop has none. Alan Shreve described what testing one Twilio app took: a phone call that crossed the phone network into Twilio’s data center, which made an HTTP request to a tunnel and on to the local service, “a really, really expensive HTTP request.” Tunneling tools already existed, and localtunnel was widely used.

Shreve wrote ngrok in Go in 2013, mostly to learn the language: “I actually built it to learn Go… I guess the third priority was to make web development easier.” Version 1 was open source under Apache 2.0 and developed from 2013 to 2016, and its inspector let developers look at and replay a request instead of triggering the webhook again. Later versions became a closed, hosted service, and the v1 repository is now archived as no longer developed or supported.

The company grew without outside money. When it raised a $50 million Series A led by Lightspeed Venture Partners in December 2022, its first fundraise, it said more than 30,000 paying customers had funded it and more than 5 million developers used it. Since then ngrok has moved from tunnels toward a general ingress platform: Traffic Policy, Cloud Endpoints, endpoint pooling and an AI Gateway, with sharing localhost as one product of three.

choices.choice: The agent dials out instead of ngrok forwarding to an IP
choices.why: Services can then run anywhere (any cloud, an on-prem data center, a Raspberry Pi, a laptop) with no DNS, ports or certificates to set up, and attackers can’t go around ngrok by finding the upstream address.
Shreve built it to learn Go, and later credited the project’s success “in no small part to choosing Go as the implementation language” and to feedback from the Go community.

choices.choice: Apply policy in ngrok’s network, not in the agent
choices.why: The agent only connects and forwards. Keeping authentication, routing and rate limits in the cloud service means one policy behaves the same for the CLI, an SDK, the Kubernetes Operator or reverse SSH.
